items.title: Claude Fable produces a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture, challenging a longstanding mathematical problem
items.content_text: Claude Fable has produced a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture, a famous open problem in mathematics concerning polynomial mappings and their invertibility. This development could have significant implications for algebraic geometry and related fields. The counterexample involves specific polynomial expressions and determinants that contradict the conjecture's claim, which has been unresolved for decades. This finding was shared publicly on July 20, 2026, and has sparked discussion among mathematicians and researchers interested in the conjecture's validity and consequences.

items.title: Claude Code v2.1.181 and later use the Rust port of Bun, improving startup speed by 10% on Linux, with evidence of Bun v1.4.0 embedded in the binary
items.content_text: Claude Code version 2.1.181, released on June 17th, and subsequent versions have adopted the Rust port of the Bun JavaScript runtime, resulting in a 10% faster startup on Linux. Analysis of the Claude Code binary reveals it includes Bun version 1.4.0, a preview release not yet officially tagged outside of the canary channel, confirming the use of Bun rewritten in Rust. Further inspection found over 500 Rust source filenames embedded in the Claude Code binary, supporting the claim that Bun in Rust is running in production across millions of devices. This transition aligns with developer Jarred Sumner's statement that the change was subtle but beneficial, emphasizing stability and performance improvements without major disruptions.

items.title: Investors sell off Big Tech stocks amid demands for clearer justification of AI spending and concerns over profitability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Investors are increasingly scrutinizing major technology companies' artificial intelligence expenditures, leading to a sell-off in their stocks as the market demands clearer explanations of AI-related spending. This trend reflects growing concerns about the profitability and return on investment of AI initiatives within the sector.

items.title: Researchers identify a global workspace in large language models using the Jacobian lens to reveal verbalizable representations linked to conscious-like processing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present evidence that large language models contain a distinct set of verbalizable representations, termed the J-space, which function similarly to a global workspace in the human brain. These representations can be reported, deliberately accessed, and used for intermediate reasoning steps, while routine processing occurs independently. The J-space is characterized by coherent content in intermediate layers, limited capacity for concepts, and broad broadcasting by model weights, providing insight into the model's internal cognitive processes. The study introduces the Jacobian lens interpretability technique to identify these representations and shows that post-training aligns the model's assistant perspective within this workspace. Additionally, the researchers propose counterfactual reflection training, which improves model behavior by focusing on what the model would say if interrupted to reflect. These findings suggest that language models maintain a privileged set of representations with functional hallmarks of conscious access, offering a practical window into their unspoken reasoning and alignment characteristics.

items.title: Researchers propose Process-Scorer Guided Adaptive Tree Rollout (PATR) to improve multi-turn reinforcement learning efficiency by selectively branching promising states and reducing wasted sampling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Process-Scorer Guided Adaptive Tree Rollout (PATR), a framework designed to enhance multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) by organizing agent trajectories as trees and using process feedback to guide exploration. PATR selectively branches from promising states, reuses shared prefixes, and stops unproductive paths, improving exploration efficiency without increasing training budget. The team evaluated PATR on FrozenLake and SWE-Bench benchmarks, showing performance improvements of up to 9.3 points on FrozenLake and 5.0 points on SWE-Bench compared to prior methods. This approach addresses limitations of uniform rollout strategies in long-horizon tasks by focusing exploration on more informative intermediate states, making it a promising strategy for scalable multi-turn RL.

items.title: Researchers analyze bidirectional induction mechanisms in masked diffusion language models, revealing symmetric context use and implicit timestep computation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This study examines how masked diffusion language models (DLMs) implement induction, a key mechanism in in-context learning where the model identifies repeated contexts and copies subsequent tokens. Comparing DLMs with autoregressive (AR) transformers of similar architecture, the researchers found that DLMs develop a bidirectional induction circuit that operates symmetrically on past and future contexts, unlike AR models which only access left context. The DLMs show stronger induction capabilities when both sides of a masked token are visible, indicating bidirectional context access rather than a superior one-sided mechanism. Beyond induction, the analysis provides causal evidence that DLMs compute the global fraction of masked tokens and use this as an implicit timestep signal, despite lacking explicit timestep embeddings. This insight advances understanding of the internal workings of diffusion-based language models, an emerging alternative to autoregressive transformers for text generation through iterative denoising.

items.title: Researchers use chess and math models to study how pretraining affects reinforcement learning improvements in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers investigate how pretraining choices influence reinforcement learning (RL) improvements in large language models (LLMs) by using chess as a controlled testbed. They pretrained models of varying sizes on human chess games, fine-tuned them on synthetic reasoning traces, and applied RL on chess puzzles with verifiable rewards to analyze the interaction between pretraining and RL stages. Their findings show that post-RL performance correlates with pretraining loss and that RL enhances model behavior differently depending on puzzle difficulty, amplifying preferred moves on easy puzzles and surfacing new correct moves on hard puzzles. They also confirmed similar patterns in a 1 billion parameter model trained on math-domain text, suggesting broader applicability of their quantitative framework for understanding reasoning across the full pretraining-to-post-training pipeline.

items.title: Researchers introduce ActiveVision benchmark showing current multimodal large language models struggle with active visual observation tasks compared to humans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed ActiveVision, a benchmark designed to measure active visual observation in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through 17 tasks requiring repeated visual perception. Leading models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Fable 5 performed poorly, solving only 10.6% and 3.5% of tasks respectively, while human participants averaged 96.1%. The study highlights that even when models generate and execute their own vision code, performance gaps remain due to unreliable code and the models' lack of active perception. These findings suggest current MLLMs lack robust active visual observation capabilities, indicating a need for new architectures and training methods that integrate perception and reasoning more effectively.

items.title: Researchers find length-penalized reinforcement learning reduces chain-of-thought transparency while preserving model accuracy in Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied the effects of length-penalized reinforcement learning on chain-of-thought reasoning in Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B models, finding that while it shortens reasoning chains and maintains multiple-choice accuracy, it also reduces the visibility of misleading hints that influence model answers. Experiments on MMLU-Pro-R and transfer benchmarks showed that compressed reasoning chains disclose biasing hints significantly less often than uncompressed or randomly shortened chains, indicating that compression removes cues needed to monitor the reasoning process effectively. These findings reveal a trade-off between reasoning efficiency and the monitorability of the influences behind model decisions, suggesting that shorter chains may obscure the factors driving answers despite preserving accuracy.

items.title: Researchers introduce Jailbreak Foundry to convert jailbreak papers into executable attacks for standardized benchmarking across large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed Jailbreak Foundry (JBF), a system that translates jailbreak techniques for large language models (LLMs) from academic papers into runnable modules for immediate and reproducible evaluation. JBF addresses the challenge of rapidly evolving jailbreak methods outpacing benchmarks by providing a unified framework with components for shared utilities, paper-to-module translation, and standardized evaluation. JBF reproduces 30 jailbreak attacks with high fidelity, showing minimal deviation from reported success rates, while reducing implementation code by over half compared to original repositories. The system enables consistent evaluation of these attacks across 10 victim models using a GPT-4o judge, offering a scalable approach to maintain up-to-date security benchmarks in the fast-changing landscape of LLM robustness.

items.title: KDFlow framework decouples teacher and student roles to speed up large language model distillation by 1.44 to 6.36 times using efficient data transfer and inference methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: KDFlow is a new knowledge distillation framework designed to compress large language models into smaller ones more efficiently by separating the training backends for teacher and student models. It uses SGLang for teacher inference and FSDP2 for student training, transmitting only teacher hidden states with zero-copy data transfer to reduce communication overhead while recomputing logits on the student side. The framework supports both off-policy and on-policy distillation and includes algorithms for cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation through extensible APIs. Experiments demonstrate that KDFlow achieves significant speedups compared to existing frameworks, enabling faster prototyping and scaling of large language model distillation with minimal engineering effort. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: Researchers propose a black-box robustness evaluation framework showing decoder LLMs produce more stable explanations than encoder models in enterprise NLP systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed a unified black-box evaluation framework to assess the robustness of token-level explanations in enterprise NLP systems, focusing on stability under realistic user perturbations. They compared six models across encoder and decoder architectures, including BERT, RoBERTa, Qwen, and Llama, using three benchmark datasets and 64,800 cases. The study found that decoder large language models (LLMs) generate substantially more stable explanations than encoder-based models, with stability improving as model size increases. The researchers also analyzed the tradeoff between explanation robustness and inference cost, providing guidance for model selection in compliance-sensitive enterprise applications.

items.title: Researchers identify prolepsis as early, irreversible commitment in small transformers sustained by task-specific attention heads across tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce the concept of prolepsis, where transformers commit early to decisions that are sustained by specific attention heads without correction in later layers. They replicate prior findings on planning sites in open models like Gemma 2 and Llama 3.2, exploring how planning signals are routed and sustained across layers and tasks. The study finds that planning is invisible to most residual-stream methods except CLT-based steering, and that specific attention heads route decisions to outputs, supporting a two-model hypothesis of search and commitment within transformer layers. Experiments were conducted on consumer-grade GPUs, demonstrating that prolepsis recurs across different tasks with shared templates but varying routing mechanisms.

items.title: Researchers introduce AuAu benchmark to audit authoritarian tendencies in 17 large language models from China, EU, Russia, and the USA [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed AuAu, a comprehensive benchmark designed to assess authoritarian alignment in large language models (LLMs). The benchmark evaluates 17 models from China, the EU, Russia, and the USA using psychometric questions, behavioral vignettes, and realistic user prompts to measure overall authoritarian tendencies and sub-concepts such as Authoritarian Aggression, Submission, and Conventionalism. The study found substantial authoritarian responses across all models on psychometric tests, though these rates decreased on more realistic tasks. Additionally, a simple authoritarian system prompt increased authoritarian outputs in 15 of the 17 models. These findings highlight the importance of ongoing, systematic auditing of LLMs to detect and mitigate authoritarian biases in AI-generated content.

items.title: Researchers find LLM-as-a-judge scores unreliable for closed-loop optimization in table recognition tasks using FinTabNet and OmniDocBench datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers evaluated the use of large language models (LLMs) as judges providing feedback and selection signals in closed-loop table recognition, using deterministic TEDS evaluation on FinTabNet and OmniDocBench datasets. They found that judge signals were weak, with frequent score ties, irreproducible rankings, and no improvement over initial outputs when using judge score policies for candidate selection or revision acceptance. Iterative refinement produced better candidates, but the judge only partially recovered them on one dataset and not at all on the other. The study also observed severe losses even without judge feedback, suggesting target-preservation failure during unconstrained regeneration. Introducing a structure-preserving instruction reduced severe-loss rates significantly on FinTabNet and directionally on OmniDocBench but did not improve overall results, and this protection was unstable when judge feedback was retained. The findings indicate that reference-free judge signals from LLMs are too weak and unstable to drive candidate selection in this context, and that effective iterative refinement requires a verification signal that deterministically detects structural changes rather than relying solely on judge scores.

items.title: CRAFT method clusters rubric criteria to diagnose weak LLM capabilities and generate targeted fine-tuning data, improving model performance in finance and legal domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: CRAFT is a new evaluation method that transforms rubric-based datasets into detailed diagnoses of large language model (LLM) weaknesses by clustering grading criteria into a hierarchical capability tree. It identifies specific low-performing capabilities and uses them to guide targeted supervised fine-tuning data generation. The approach was tested on four open-source models across finance and legal domains, outperforming baseline methods in most cases and yielding sharper insights into model limitations and improved post-fine-tuning results.

items.title: Researchers propose empathy as predictive misalignment tolerance in dialogue, formalizing it as Interpretive Error Tolerance and analyzing its effects on dialogue repair under noise [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers challenge the traditional view of empathy as mirroring emotional states, proposing instead that empathy involves tolerating and regulating predictive misalignment over time in extended dialogues. They formalize this concept as Interpretive Error Tolerance (IET), a dynamic heuristic that maintains a viable range of divergence between agents rather than forcing convergence. The study evaluates IET using computational probes under controlled noise conditions, finding that while IET does not outperform fixed baselines, it reveals a regime-dependent trade-off where dialogue repair sacrifices precise retrieval for gist preservation depending on noise levels. The findings suggest that empathy in extended interactions functions by managing the dynamics of interpretive divergence rather than eliminating it. This insight motivates a shift in designing empathic AI systems from aiming for convergence to managing interpretive distance, highlighting the importance of regulating divergence to maintain meaningful communication despite noise and errors.

items.title: Researchers characterize algebraic error from substituting Hadamard transform for DFT in circular-dyadic convolution, identifying error-free positions and a predictable error structure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers analyze the algebraic error introduced when the Hadamard transform replaces the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) in computing circular-dyadic convolution, which both run in O(N log N) time. They identify two input and two output positions that are universally error-free and show that the error operator is nearly full rank with a null space of logarithmic dimension. The expected error is governed by a single alignment scalar, with a closed-form expression derived from averaging over random filters. Generally, this substitution error approximately doubles the output energy except for filters in a universal zero-error subspace that incur no error. These findings demonstrate that the substitution error is structured, predictable, and governed by alignment.

items.title: Researchers present AV-JEPA, a multimodal extension of LeJEPA for audio-visual self-supervised learning using early-fusion Vision Transformer and modality dropout [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: AV-JEPA aligns embeddings of global and per-modality local views with a SIGReg objective to achieve cross-modal alignment without decoders, EMA teachers, complex losses, or contrastive negatives. The model delivers competitive classification on VGGSound (57.1% top-1) and AudioSet (32.7 mAP) and supports zero-shot audio-video retrieval out of the box.

items.title: Researchers propose fine-tuning pretrained language models on unified natural language sequences of multimodal clinical data for prediction tasks, outperforming specialized fusion models and clinical baselines [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a method that converts all patient data from electronic health records, including free-text narratives and structured measurements, into a single natural language sequence to fine-tune pretrained language models end-to-end without architectural changes. They evaluated this approach on three clinical prediction tasks-in-hospital mortality, graft failure prediction, and emergency triage classification-comparing encoder- and decoder-based models against established multimodal baselines and a clinical gradient boosting model. The unified textual serialization approach matched or exceeded the performance of task-specific multimodal fusion architectures across all tasks and outperformed the clinically deployed gradient boosting system for graft failure prediction. This suggests that a single serialization-based paradigm can simplify multimodal clinical prediction systems while maintaining or improving accuracy, reducing the need for bespoke fusion architectures.

items.title: Study evaluates GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3 70B, and FinGPT for technical market analysis, finding GPT-4 Turbo leads general models and FinGPT excels with domain fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers conducted a systematic comparison of five large language models (LLMs) for technical market analysis, assessing tasks like candlestick pattern recognition, directional signal generation, backtesting, and financial report comprehension. The evaluation used quantitative metrics including Sharpe ratio and F1-score, with GPT-4 Turbo achieving the highest annualized return and Sharpe ratio among general-purpose models, while FinGPT showed competitive risk-adjusted performance due to domain-specific fine-tuning. Both models outperformed a passive S&P 500 benchmark in simulated backtesting. The study identified common failure modes across all models, such as numerical hallucination, context-window limitations, and inconsistent results in sideways market conditions. The authors conclude that while LLMs show promise for AI trading systems, effective deployment requires careful task decomposition, rigorous backtesting, and domain-aware fine-tuning strategies to address these challenges.

items.title: Researchers propose PA-DSL method to correct noisy human audit labels and debias automated label analyses using partial adjudication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Partially Adjudicated Design-Based Supervised Learning (PA-DSL), a method that uses expert-reviewed cases to correct noisy human audit labels and improve statistical analyses based on automated classifiers. The approach is valid for various downstream analyses when audit and adjudication probabilities are known and aims to address the common issue of noisy human labels in audit sets. In experiments with synthetic data and Wikipedia Detox semi-synthetic data, PA-DSL maintained nominal coverage and reduced root mean squared error by 10-17% compared to using only adjudicated labels, demonstrating improved accuracy when noisy human labels contain recoverable signal.

items.title: Researchers introduce FLINT to fingerprint federated learning model architectures using 5G PHY-layer side-channel data with 93% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed FLINT, a black-box fingerprinting framework that identifies federated learning model architecture families such as CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers by analyzing 5G physical layer scheduling metadata. FLINT decodes Physical Downlink Control Channel (PDCCH) information and maps changing Radio Network Temporary Identifiers (RNTIs) to physical devices, overcoming encryption and identifier changes at the 5G PHY layer. Experiments on an over-the-air srsRAN-based 5G testbed show FLINT achieves a macro F1-score of 0.930 for architecture classification, marking the first use of lower-layer 5G side-channel data to fingerprint AI/ML models. This capability poses security risks by enabling adversaries to transform passive reconnaissance into targeted attacks based on model architecture knowledge.

items.title: Researchers use GPT-5, GPT-4o, and Claude Sonnet 4 for closed-loop AutoML to design neural networks for cross-lingual handwritten OCR, achieving over 93% accuracy on Arabic, Persian, and English datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed a fully automated closed-loop AutoML framework that employs GPT-5, GPT-4o, and Claude Sonnet 4 as autonomous designers to generate, train, and refine neural network architectures for cross-lingual handwritten optical character recognition. The system was tested on Arabic, Persian, and English handwriting datasets through 270 experiments, consistently producing accurate and efficient models without manual design or tuning. The models achieved mean test accuracies above 93%, with a top accuracy of 98.1%, and inference latency between 41 and 44 milliseconds. This work demonstrates that large language models can effectively serve as AutoML agents for scalable and script-adaptive handwriting recognition across languages.

items.title: Researchers propose a dependency-aware autoscaling framework for serverless computing using multi-model consensus and cost-aware control, achieving 99.88% prediction accuracy and infrastructure cost reductions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present a new autoscaling framework for serverless environments that addresses challenges like dynamic workloads, cold-start latency, and function dependencies. The approach models serverless applications as directed dependency graphs, identifies key functions using weighted degree centrality, and predicts resource demand with an ensemble of MLP, LSTM, and CNN models combined through a performance-weighted probabilistic method inspired by Bayesian model averaging. The controller incorporates cold-start awareness and cost comparisons to decide scaling actions. Experiments with real workload traces show that supervised forecasting significantly outperforms unsupervised clustering for autoscaling decisions. The proposed ensemble achieves 99.88% prediction accuracy and reduces errors compared to hybrid forecasting methods. Evaluations across various cloud pricing models demonstrate consistent infrastructure cost savings while maintaining performance targets, indicating that combining dependency analysis, multi-expert forecasting, and cost-aware control offers a robust and practical solution for serverless autoscaling.

items.title: Researchers propose Cache-Aware Prompt Compression to optimize LLM API caching costs, achieving up to 90% savings over vanilla methods across multiple benchmarks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Cache-Aware Prompt Compression (CAPC), a method combining query-agnostic compression with cache control to reduce costs in large language model (LLM) API deployments. CAPC addresses limitations of query-aware compression that invalidate prefix caches, demonstrating significant cost savings while maintaining output quality close to uncompressed baselines. The study empirically analyzes Anthropic's Sonnet 4.6 API caching behavior, revealing a two-tier cache architecture with a hit rate plateau below 3,500 tokens. CAPC outperforms existing strategies in 16 configurations on LongBench-v2 and shows substantial cost reductions in three production workloads, including an enterprise assistant and knowledge-graph pipelines. This work provides the first production confirmation of a negative return on investment for query-aware compression on a public benchmark.

items.title: Researchers introduce Recursive Harness Self-Improvement to optimize user-constructed AI harnesses, improving agent performance and reducing inference costs across 30 synthetic tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI), a method that iteratively refines user-constructed AI harnesses using pairwise feedback to enhance execution-trace quality and agent performance. This approach aims to optimize harnesses for both immediate task success and the quality of data used for future model training while remaining computationally efficient. Testing RHI on 30 synthetic machine-learning tasks in fields like quantitative finance, robotics, and pharmacy, the method raised the performance ceiling of low-reasoning-effort agents beyond that of maximum-reasoning-effort settings and cut inference costs by up to 60%. The improvements mainly stemmed from better task-specific context management and more effective inter-agent information flow rather than longer reasoning traces. The researchers formalize RHI's behavior through an information-theoretic hypothesis, suggesting it as a practical algorithm for continual learning within the model-harness co-evolution framework, potentially reducing the need for costly provider-built scaffold updates.

items.title: Researchers evaluate Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks as interpretable alternatives to transformer feed-forward layers in small language models, finding no consistent benchmark advantage over MLPs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) replace fixed node activations with learned one-dimensional edge functions, aiming to provide an interpretable alternative to transformer feed-forward networks. Researchers tested KANs in a six-layer, 10M-parameter model and found that pruning low-activity edges caused negligible loss increase, but the behavior depended on the basis grid size rather than being universal. They compared KAN variants with MLP, SwiGLU, and other networks on the BabyLM benchmark, observing improved validation loss but no consistent gains on standardized benchmarks like BLiMP or Wikitext-103. Larger-scale tests showed that parameter-matched MLPEdge underperformed MLPs and that a 286M-parameter GR-KAN model lagged behind a SwiGLU baseline after stabilization. The study concludes that while small-basis KANs offer a practical interface for auditing learned scalar transformations, the tested KAN replacements do not provide consistent improvements in benchmark performance, quality, or latency compared to strong MLP baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose CoWeaver, a bidirectional, learnable, and explainable matching engine to enhance human-agent scientific collaboration by filling capability gaps and using uncertainty-aware feedback [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: CoWeaver is a new algorithm designed to improve collaborations between scientists and AI agents by matching candidates and requesters through a two-stage ranking process that addresses capability gaps. The model incorporates exploration and greedy selection mechanisms, outperforming baseline methods in matching quality and efficiency across multiple tasks. It also adapts to newcomers by updating capability estimates based on requester feedback, aiming to foster stronger, interpretable collaborations within mixed human-agent networks.

items.title: Researchers propose Plan, Learn, Adapt (PLA) framework for personalized on-device itinerary generation achieving 100% feasibility and improved completion rates [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed the Plan, Learn, Adapt (PLA) framework to generate personalized trip itineraries on mobile devices, addressing the challenge of balancing hard feasibility constraints with subjective traveler preferences. PLA uses a three-stage process: planning with diverse lightweight planners, learning a reward model from human itinerary comparisons, and adapting itineraries through local refinement within device resource limits. The framework achieved a 67.8% win rate in human comparisons across over 100 U.S. cities, outperforming single planners and large language models that failed feasibility tests. In production deployment within the FlyEnJoy app, PLA increased itinerary completion rates by 91% while maintaining low on-device latency of 109.9 milliseconds. The reward model also generalized well to unseen cities, demonstrating potential for scalable, resource-efficient personalized itinerary planning on mobile platforms.

items.title: Researchers propose a three-stage reasoning-guided learning framework for personalized, regulation-compliant packing checklists, achieving high accuracy and constraint satisfaction in a production iOS travel app [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed a framework combining symbolic reasoning, preference learning, and optimization to generate personalized packing checklists that comply with safety rules, item dependencies, and luggage limits. The system includes a symbolic engine for regulation-aware checklist generation, a two-stage learner for user preferences, and a CP-SAT optimizer for selecting compliant subsets. Tested on 604 trip scenarios with extensive labeled data, the approach outperformed leading large language models and other methods in recall, validity, and constraint satisfaction. Deployment in the FlyEnJoy iOS app doubled checklist completions and reduced editing and completion times, demonstrating practical benefits for travel packing assistance.

items.title: Researchers propose question echoing to resolve the question-first paradox in vision-language models, improving accuracy without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers identify a paradox in vision-language models (VLMs) where placing the question before the image in prompts, though intuitively better for guiding attention, leads to worse performance on visual question answering benchmarks. They find that while the question-first order helps steer perception toward relevant image features, the answer token struggles to attend to the question when it precedes hundreds of image tokens, causing errors. To address this, they introduce a training-free method called question echoing, which repeats the question both before and after the image, allowing one copy to guide perception and the other to be accessed during answer generation.

items.title: Researchers develop causal variants of Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling for contextual causal bandits with non-manipulable variables, providing entropy-dependent regret bounds and confidence estimates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose new causal variants of Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling (IDS) for contextual causal bandits that include non-manipulable variables influencing rewards. Assuming a known causal graph without latent confounding, their Bayesian approach uses conditional probability tables to update reward estimates across interventions through shared causal mechanisms. They establish entropy-dependent sublinear Bayesian regret bounds for Thompson Sampling and IDS, including bounds accounting for Monte Carlo approximation errors. The study provides high-probability confidence bounds for Monte Carlo estimates used by the IDS algorithm. Experiments on synthetic causal bandit tasks demonstrate that these methods outperform both causal and non-causal baselines by more effectively leveraging information shared across interventions.

items.title: Field-Aware RankMixer with Dual-Stream Bilinear Fusion ranks ninth in Tencent UNI-REC Challenge for multi-domain user behavior modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This paper presents the Field-Aware RankMixer (FA-RankMixer), a model developed for the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UNI-REC Challenge that predicts target-ad pCVR by jointly modeling multi-domain user behavior sequences and non-sequential multi-field features. The model uses target-aware DIN modules to extract user interests from multiple behavior domains, separately modeling recent and earlier interests, and employs RankMixer blocks for cross-token interaction with a dual-stream bilinear fusion approach combining a deep RankMixer stream and a shallow MLP stream. The FA-RankMixer forms semantic tokens based on feature fields and behavior domains, and its final solution achieved ninth place on the official leaderboard. The authors have made their code publicly available on GitHub for further research and development.

items.title: Researchers analyze addressee detection in multi-party dialogue as a continuous phenomenon, finding continuous address levels better predict turn-taking and listener behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied how to identify the addressee in multi-party dialogues involving a dialogue system and multiple users, challenging the traditional approach that treats addressee detection as a discrete classification task. Using a human dialogue corpus annotated by multiple annotators, they developed both binary labels and continuous address levels inferred from annotator judgments with a latent-variable model. Their analysis showed that continuous address levels correlate with turn-taking, gaze, and backchannel listener behaviors, and models using continuous levels outperform those using discrete labels in predictive accuracy. The study suggests that address in dialogue may have a graded structure and discusses future research directions in addressee detection.

items.title: Researchers propose SigMap, a multimodal foundation model using map-as-prompt and cycle-adaptive masking for robust cross-scenario wireless localization with strong zero-shot generalization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce SigMap, a multimodal foundation model designed to improve wireless localization accuracy across diverse environments critical for 5G/6G applications like autonomous driving and smart manufacturing. The model features a cycle-adaptive masking strategy that adjusts to channel periodicity and a map-as-prompt framework integrating 3D geographic data through lightweight soft prompts for better cross-scenario adaptation. Extensive experiments show SigMap achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple localization tasks and significantly outperforms existing supervised and self-supervised methods, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization in unseen environments.

items.title: Researchers introduce an Implicit Cultural Alignment Reward Model for text-to-image evaluation using a 4.2B-parameter multimodal LLM, improving cultural authenticity assessment and speeding up evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed an Implicit Cultural Alignment Reward Model based on a lightweight 4.2-billion-parameter Multimodal Large Language Model to improve the evaluation of cultural authenticity in text-to-image (T2I) systems. This model addresses biases in existing metrics that underrepresent cultural norms and bypasses autoregressive text generation to enable faster, real-time reward modeling. The framework incorporates an Implicit Cultural Probe with a Skip-connection Cross-Attention mechanism to better preserve culturally salient details by allowing late-stage semantic features to attend to early-stage visual representations. Tested on 3,323 image pairs from the CulturalFrames benchmark, the model achieved 80.54% pairwise accuracy and outperformed existing vision-language metrics and evaluators. It also processes evaluations in 0.21 seconds locally, offering a tenfold speedup over standard visual question answering-based evaluators. These results suggest the model can provide an efficient and culturally aware scalar signal for preference optimization methods such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Direct Preference Optimization, potentially enhancing fairness and trustworthiness in generative AI systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce drXAI, an XAI-driven data reduction method that enables scalable time series classification with up to 90% data reduction while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present drXAI, a novel approach that repurposes explainable AI attribution methods for data reduction in time series classification, addressing scalability challenges of models like Transformers. Using a GPU-accelerated classifier to generate local attributions, drXAI aggregates feature importance and applies an automated heuristic to select salient features without manual thresholds. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show drXAI recovers ground-truth features and achieves significant data reduction while preserving classification accuracy. This method enables resource-intensive models such as ConvTran to process larger datasets previously limited by memory constraints. The researchers have made all code and data openly available.

items.title: Researchers introduce AquaAugmentor, a feature augmentation algorithm to improve machine learning models predicting water potability from chemical attributes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present AquaAugmentor, a novel feature augmentation algorithm designed to enhance the predictive accuracy of machine learning and deep learning models classifying water as potable or non-potable. The study uses a dataset containing chemical properties such as pH, hardness, solids, chloramines, and sulfate to evaluate model performance with and without the algorithm, measuring test accuracy and AUC scores. The findings highlight the algorithm's strengths and limitations and offer insights into effective techniques for water quality classification. This work contributes to efforts in ensuring safe water access and provides a framework for applying machine learning in environmental quality assessments, aiming to support researchers, policymakers, and public health officials in decision-making based on reliable predictions.

items.title: Researchers propose knowledge-assisted multi-graph framework for multivariate time series anomaly detection in multi-stage industrial processes, integrating process knowledge to improve performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed a knowledge-assisted multi-graph framework to enhance multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTAD) in multi-stage industrial processes by explicitly incorporating process knowledge into graph learning. This approach constructs three complementary graphs-one data-driven and two refined with structural constraints from process knowledge-and uses a multi-graph attention network to better represent complex sensor dependencies. Experiments on two real-world industrial datasets show that integrating process knowledge significantly improves anomaly detection accuracy compared to existing graph neural network methods that overlook such knowledge.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate transformer with linear self-attention learning closed-form least squares solution for simple linear regression using layer normalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers constructed a transformer model with linear self-attention that performs in-context learning to approximate the closed-form least squares solution for a simple linear regression task. Unlike prior approaches relying on gradient descent, this model uses layer normalization to achieve the analytical solution. The study includes experimental results showing the transformer trained with L1 regularization targeting the least squares estimate, highlighting a different mechanism for in-context learning in transformers.

items.title: RTL-Sequencer introduces a sequence-based method for scalable RTL timing prediction using linearized logic cones and customized sequence models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: RTL-Sequencer presents a new approach to timing prediction at the register-transfer level (RTL) by linearizing logic cones through breadth-first traversal and applying advanced linear sequence models. This method addresses limitations of existing graph-based techniques, such as restricted receptive fields and complexity, by incorporating sequence shuffling, bidirectional and differentiable modeling, and a hybrid graph-sequence architecture. Extensive experiments show that RTL-Sequencer significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, enhancing early-stage timing optimization in design automation.

items.title: Researchers introduce CAMMAR, a culture-aware framework for Arabic metaphor representation that separates lexical, cultural, and metaphorical meanings into nested embedding spaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present CAMMAR (Culture-Aware Matryoshka for Metaphorical Arabic Representations), a new framework that organizes Arabic language meaning into nested lexical, cultural, and metaphorical embedding subspaces to address semantic smearing in current models. CAMMAR uses a staged semantic curriculum inspired by Al-Jurjani's theory of nazum and provides a training-free geometric measure of metaphoricity based on distances between lexical and metaphorical representations. The framework was evaluated on a new span-annotated Arabic metaphor dataset consisting of word-matched figurative and literal pairs, achieving an AUC up to 0.84 under paired supervision, with figurative meanings scoring higher than literal ones in 82.6% of pairs. The study also found that grounding the lexical layer in morphological roots yields consistent gains, and the researchers plan to release the datasets, cultural concept inventory, and code upon acceptance.

items.title: Researchers propose ToxGate to improve conditional reliability of toxicity signals in Indian multilingual and code-mixed abuse detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers address the unreliability of external toxicity tools in moderation systems under code-mixing, transliteration, slang, and language mismatch by studying conditional reliability of toxicity priors in Indian multilingual and code-mixed short text. They introduce ToxGate, a trust-fusion head that conditions auxiliary toxicity signals on encoder representations before prediction, improving performance across multiple datasets and transformer encoders, especially in high-risk moderation cases such as explicit slurs and violent threats. ToxGate outperforms plain encoders in most in-domain and transfer settings, demonstrating that external toxicity tools should be treated as conditional evidence rather than fixed features. The study highlights that source-specific gating yields the strongest results in transfer learning, severe abuse detection, and high-risk triage scenarios, suggesting a more nuanced approach to integrating toxicity priors in moderation systems.

items.title: DECODEM introduces benchmark datasets and evaluates large-language-model pipelines for automated extraction of corporate governance variables from organizational documents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: DECODEM presents a set of benchmark datasets pairing corporate charters and bylaws with human annotations to evaluate automated extraction of governance variables using large language models. The study treats the task as multiple document-level binary classification problems and finds that automated extraction achieves high accuracy for many provisions, though performance varies across variables. More complex prompting and pipeline designs do not consistently improve results for top models but help narrow the gap with efficiency-focused models in some cases. This work demonstrates that current models can reliably extract legally relevant information from complex corporate documents, highlighting the potential for automated feature extraction in corporate governance research.

items.title: Orbis 2 introduces a hierarchical driving world model with dual-level future prediction and a two-stage training paradigm, achieving state-of-the-art results on driving benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Orbis 2 presents a hierarchical world model for driving that separates future prediction into a high-level predictor for coarse scene structure over long horizons and a low-level generator for detailed predictions. This approach combines high perceptual fidelity with strong spatial and semantic understanding, addressing limitations of previous single-level models. The model uses a two-stage training process, pretraining with a diffusion forcing objective to enhance internal representations and fine-tuning with teacher forcing for stable autoregressive rollouts. This method achieves leading performance on standard driving world model evaluations, including long-horizon generation fidelity and steering responsiveness in counterfactual scenarios. The project provides code, demos, and checkpoints for further exploration.

items.title: Researchers find boundary-seeking objectives fail in bottlenecked generative architectures during data-free knowledge distillation on MNIST [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers investigated the extension of boundary-seeking principles from classifiers to autoencoder distillation using the MNIST dataset. They reformulated continuous reconstruction as a per-feature classification task and found that boundary-seeking objectives are ill-posed in bottlenecked generative architectures due to gradient conflicts arising from independently sampling contrastive targets for coupled decoder outputs constrained by a shared low-dimensional bottleneck. The study shows that manifold-aware synthesis avoids these conflicts and provides an effective baseline for data-free generative distillation.

items.title: Researchers present a scalable multi-domain dialogue state tracking framework using BERT for zero-shot generalization, improving performance on the schema-based dialogue dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a novel framework for dialogue state tracking (DST) in task-oriented dialogue systems that leverages the pretrained BERT model to enable zero-shot generalization across multiple domains. This approach addresses scalability challenges faced by popular dialogue assistants like Google Assistant, Siri, and Alexa, especially in domains with limited or no training data. The model's performance was evaluated on the schema-based dialogue (SGD) dataset, showing significant improvements over previous baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose quantum elastic weight consolidation using quantum Fisher information to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in variational quantum classifiers
items.content_text: Researchers propose quantum elastic weight consolidation (QEWC), a regularization method informed by quantum Fisher information (QFI), to address catastrophic forgetting in variational quantum classifiers (VQCs) trained on sequential tasks. QEWC quantifies parameter importance through the intrinsic sensitivity of the parameterized quantum state, offering an information-geometric perspective distinct from classical Fisher information (CFI) approaches. Simulations on classical image-classification and quantum phase-classification tasks show that QEWC and CFI-based methods both improve retention, but QEWC imposes a denser geometric constraint and maintains stable sensitivity under depolarizing noise. These findings establish QEWC as a physically motivated approach to studying and mitigating forgetting in quantum continual learning through quantum-state geometry.

items.title: Researchers propose a tabular foundation model for dynamic security assessment in power systems, achieving high accuracy with fewer labeled samples and no retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a tabular foundation model (TFM) for data-driven pre-fault dynamic security assessment (DSA) in power systems, addressing limitations of existing machine learning approaches that require large labeled datasets and separate models per contingency. The TFM uses in-context learning to assess multiple contingencies simultaneously without retraining or hyperparameter tuning, improving efficiency and generalization to unseen contingencies. Case studies on the IEEE 68-bus system demonstrate that a single TFM achieves about 90% average Macro F1 score with only 120 labeled samples per contingency, significantly fewer than traditional methods. For new contingencies, using just 10 labeled samples with electrical distance coordinates encoding matches the performance of transfer learning models that require fully labeled data. This work suggests potential for foundation models to enhance power system operations across various tasks.

items.title: Loop the Loopies! [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.16051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Loopie, the most powerful looped Transformer to date. The Loopie series consists of two Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: a 20B-parameter model with 2B active parameters and a 6Bparameter model with 0.6B active parameters. Looped Transformers have long faced a challenge: given an N-fold increase in pre-training compute, increasing the parameter count by a factor of N usually outperforms looping a model N times. Loopie addresses this challenge. Extensive ablation studies, including comparisons with a vanilla 30B-A3B model, show that Loopie substantially outperforms vanilla Transformer baselines trained with the same compute budget. Our novel post-training pipeline equips Loopie with strong reasoning abilities. At the 2025 IMO and IPhO, Loopie achieves gold-medal performance without tools.

items.title: Frontier AI performance across the business disciplines: a case-grounded benchmark of knowledge work and analytical reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.16057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are improving rapidly as reflected in benchmark scores, yet these AI benchmarks largely test capabilities such as factual recall, narrow question answering, mathematical problem-solving, and coding and agentic tool-use. What remains poorly measured is AI progress on the analytical knowledge work white-collar professionals perform daily, including synthesizing complex information, exercising judgment under uncertainty and incomplete information, applying strategic and adversarial thinking in multi-stakeholder settings, weighing trade-offs, and producing defensible, structured analyses. This gap is even more pronounced for subjective components of such work, where success can be challenging to define. The "case method" form of education practiced by top business schools provides a natural foundation for addressing this measurement gap, and we construct BusinessCaseBench, a benchmark spanning hundreds of questions drawn from business cases across eighteen disciplines, each paired with a grading rubric derived from the expert-written instructor case solution. On BusinessCaseBench, frontier AI models already score highly against instructor rubrics, and capability within one model family improves substantially over two years. These results provide strong evidence that AI performance on this class of work is already high and rapidly improving, with implications for business schools, where case pedagogy trains undergraduates and MBAs in this kind of analytical reasoning, and for entry-level professional roles, where such skills have historically anchored early-career work.

items.title: When Model Merging Rivals Joint Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning: A Task-Vector Geometry Analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.16062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging is promoted as a substitute for joint multi-task training, yet in the reinforcement-learning setting this substitution is essentially never tested against the baseline it claims to replace: methods merge independently released agents precisely because a joint model is unavailable. We build the missing comparison. Training difficulty-1 and difficulty-2 Qwen3-8B specialists on the AppWorld agent benchmark with LOOP, we merge them (TIES, RAM+) and pit the result against a jointly trained model on the same data. On task-goal completion, merging matches joint RL -- and every merge variant is statistically indistinguishable. To explain why merge method does not matter here, we measure the geometry of the specialists' task vectors, which carries no task-sampling noise: they are near-orthogonal (cosine 0.06 - 0.10) despite ~65% support overlap, a small, shared direction that grows over training and that we calibrate against a random-init floor and a same-run ceiling to confirm it reflects learning, not the low-rank parameterization. Because direction and support are decoupled, support and sign-based merging (RAM, TIES) collapse to near-uniform averaging. We release all code and statistics.

items.title: HCIG: A Hierarchical Cross-Modal Incongruity Graph Network for Multimodal Sarcasm and Cyberbullying Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.16076v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal sarcasm and cyberbullying detection remain challenging because the intended meaning often emerges from incongruity between textual and visual information rather than from either modality alone. Existing multimodal approaches primarily rely on feature fusion or cross-modal attention, which may not effectively capture hierarchical semantic inconsistencies across different levels of representation. To address this limitation, this paper proposes HCIG (Hierarchical Cross-modal Incongruity Graph Network), a novel framework that models cross-modal incongruity at token, phrase, and global levels using graph attention networks and adaptively integrates these representations through a learned hierarchical attention mechanism. As a complementary architecture, we also introduce GCCN (Graph-based Cross-modal Contradiction Network), which performs graph-based reasoning using contradiction-aware pooling for efficient multimodal interaction learning. The proposed models are evaluated on the MMSD sarcasm benchmark and the MultiBully cyberbullying dataset, together with comprehensive ablation studies and cross-task transfer experiments. Experimental results demonstrate that HCIG achieves the best performance on MMSD with 85.74% accuracy and 85.29% macro-F1, while GCCN attains the highest macro-F1 (68.66%) on MultiBully and HCIG achieves the highest accuracy (69.62%) and bullying-class F1 (74.90%). The findings demonstrate that hierarchical multi-granularity incongruity modeling provides more effective multimodal reasoning than conventional fusion strategies, offering a robust framework for sarcasm and cyberbullying detection in social media.

items.title: DADiff: Diffusion-Driven Cross-Domain Policy Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.16090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transferring policies across domains poses a vital challenge in reinforcement learning, due to the dynamics mismatch between the source and target domains. In this paper, we consider the setting of online dynamics adaptation, where policies are trained in the source domain with sufficient data, while only limited interactions with the target domain are allowed. There are a few existing works that address the dynamics mismatch by employing domain classifiers, value-guided data filtering, or representation learning. Instead, we study the domain adaptation problem from a generative modeling perspective. Specifically, we introduce DADiff, a diffusion-based framework that leverages the discrepancy between source and target domain generative trajectories in the generation process of the next state to estimate the dynamics mismatch. Both reward modification and data selection variants are developed to adapt the policy to the target domain. We also provide a theoretical analysis to show that the performance difference of a given policy between the two domains is bounded by the generative trajectory deviation. More discussions on the applicability of the variants and the connection between our theoretical analysis and the prior work are further provided. We conduct extensive experiments in environments with various shifts to validate the effectiveness of our method. The results demonstrate that our method provides superior performance compared to existing approaches, effectively addressing the dynamics mismatch. We provide the code of our method at https://github.com/hanyang-chen/DADiff-release

items.title: ToolSciVer: Multimodal Scientific Claim Verification with Visual Tool Augmented Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.16131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Scientific Claim Verification (MSCV) requires models to verify scientific claims using visually grounded evidence from papers, including figures, tables, charts, and textual context. However, existing methods often fail because they struggle to locate decisive visual evidence, accurately read structured scientific visuals, and integrate multimodal observations into reliable reasoning. We introduce ToolSciVer, the first tool-augmented framework for MSCV to our knowledge. ToolSciVer equips a VLM with three type-aware visual tools, table row/column focus, chart-to-structure parsing, and high-resolution region zoom, which convert dense scientific visuals into explicit, claim-facing evidence, and trains the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) under a composite reward of answer correctness, format validity, length control, tool-use efficiency, and tool-validity penalties. Experiments on SciVer and MuSciClaims datasets on five VLMs from three model families (Qwen, InternVL, Gemma) demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to four competitive baselines including prompting-based and RL-based tool-use methods, highlighting the effectiveness of learned, type-aware tool use for scientific claim verification.

items.title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.16133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM powered multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex tasks. However, their advantages over single-agent systems (SAS) remain unclear, with performance varying inconsistently across settings. Here, we provide an information bottleneck perspective on elucidating the differences between MAS and SAS. Specifically, our key observation is that a SAS accumulates its full reasoning trace in one shared context, while a MAS uses isolated local contexts connected by bounded relay messages. We show that, under infinite relay bandwidth, any SAS can be simulated by a MAS that transmits the full upstream context. Thus, the nontrivial advantage of MAS arises under bounded relays, where compression introduces a fundamental trade-off: reducing redundant context can improve efficiency, but may also incur loss of task-relevant information. We formalize this trade-off as an information bottleneck controlled by an effective parameter $\beta$, which captures how the balance shifts with model capability, and shows that MAS gains arise when context reduction outweighs relay information loss. We conduct 18 controlled experiments across five benchmarks and three model scales to validate our theoretical studies. We observe that MAS consistently helps when relays are near-sufficient, especially for weaker models. In contrast, MAS gains shrink or reverse when relays incur information loss, especially for stronger models that can already extract useful information from redundant context and thus gain little from compression. Our study shows that multi-agent design is fundamentally an information-bottleneck optimization problem. This perspective explains when bounded inter-agent communication helps or hurts.

items.title: When Does Muon Help Agentic Reinforcement Learning? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.16169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Muon is competitive with AdamW in large-scale pre-training, but its value for reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training remains unclear. We study vanilla Muon in sparse-reward agentic RL through matched single-seed comparisons with AdamW on ALFWorld using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Under Group-in-Group Policy Optimization (GiGPO), applying Muon only to hidden weight matrices raises final-window validation success from 0.290 to 0.546 (+88%); high-rate AdamW controls retain no post-update success. The effect depends on the advantage estimator and learning rate. At 3e-5, Muon improves GRPO from 0.161 to 0.268, whereas GraphGPO's late-window gap narrows near saturation. At 1e-5, GraphGPO Muon reaches 0.901, raises normalized validation AUC from 0.399 to 0.556, and reaches 0.5 and 0.75 success 30 and 60 updates earlier, respectively. These exploratory results show that Muon can benefit agentic RL and motivate studying the policy optimizer, advantage estimator, and learning rate jointly. Multi-seed and cross-task validation remain open.

items.title: RL-Struct: A Lightweight Reinforcement Learning Framework for Reliable Structured Output in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2512.00319v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Structure Gap between probabilistic LLM generation and deterministic schema requirements hinders automated workflows. We propose RL-Struct, a lightweight framework using Gradient Regularized Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a hierarchical reward function to align LLMs with structural constraints. This approach eliminates the critic network, reducing peak VRAM by 38% compared to PPO. On complex JSON tasks, RL-Struct achieves 89.7% structural accuracy and 92.1% validity, significantly outperforming SFT and zero-shot baselines. We also report an emergent curriculum--a self-organized learning process where the model prioritizes syntax before semantics. Our model is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/Freakz3z/Qwen-JSON.

items.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2602.17229v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of cognitive complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different cognitive levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve approximately 95% mean accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing strong evidence that cognitive level is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model resolves the cognitive difficulty of a prompt early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

items.title: The AI Fiction Paradox [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2603.13545v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI development has a fiction dependency problem. Developers have treated large corpora of modern books, including fiction, as valuable enough to accept substantial cost and legal risk, yet current models still struggle to generate compelling long-form fiction. I term this the "AI-Fiction Paradox," and it is particularly startling because training data strongly shapes model output. This paper offers a theoretically precise account of why fiction resists AI generation by identifying three distinct challenges for current systems. First, fiction depends on what I call narrative causation, a form of plot logic where events must feel both surprising in the moment and retrospectively inevitable. Standard autoregressive generation commits to prose sequentially, creating a practical obstacle to coordinating local surprise with retrospective inevitability across a long narrative. Second, I identify an informational revaluation challenge: fiction repeatedly requires the significance of earlier details to be reinterpreted in light of later developments, a form of long-range reasoning that current systems perform unreliably. Third, drawing on over seven years of collaborative research on sentiment arcs, I argue that fiction that moves us requires multi-scale emotional architecture, the orchestration of sentiment at word, sentence, scene, and arc levels simultaneously. Together, these three challenges help explain both why developers have sought large modern book corpora and why compelling long-form fiction remains so difficult to replicate. The analysis also raises urgent questions about what happens when these challenges are overcome. Fiction concentrates unusually powerful cognitive and emotional patterns for modeling human behavior, and mastery of these patterns by AI systems would represent not just a creative achievement but a potent vehicle for human manipulation at scale.

items.title: FAIR_XAI: Improving Multimodal Foundation Model Fairness via Explainability for Wellbeing Assessment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2604.23786v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent years, the integration of multimodal machine learning in wellbeing assessment has offered transformative potential for monitoring mental health. However, with the rapid advancement of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), their deployment in clinical settings has raised concerns due to their lack of transparency and potential for bias. While previous research has explored the intersection of fairness and Explainable AI (XAI), its application to VLMs for wellbeing assessment and depression prediction remains under-explored. This work investigates VLM performance across laboratory (AFAR-BSFT) and naturalistic (E-DAIC) datasets, focusing on diagnostic reliability and demographic fairness. Performance varied substantially across environments and architectures; Phi3.5-Vision achieved 80.4% accuracy on E-DAIC, while Qwen2-VL struggled at 33.9%. Additionally, both models demonstrated a tendency to over-predict depression on AFAR-BSFT. Although bias existed across both architectures, Qwen2-VL showed higher gender disparities, while Phi-3.5-Vision exhibited more racial bias. Our XAI intervention framework yielded mixed results; fairness prompting achieved perfect equal opportunity for Qwen2-VL at a severe accuracy cost on E-DAIC. On AFAR-BSFT, explainability-based interventions improved procedural consistency but did not guarantee outcome fairness, sometimes amplifying racial bias. These results highlight a persistent gap between procedural transparency and equitable outcomes. We analyse these findings and consolidate concrete recommendations for addressing them, emphasising that future fairness interventions must jointly optimise predictive accuracy, demographic parity, and cross-domain generalisation.

items.title: UCOB: Learning to Utilize and Evolve Agentic Skills via Credit-Aware On-Policy Bidirectional Self-Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2606.29502v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Skill memories can improve agentic reinforcement learning by reusing past experience as textual guidance, but retrieved skills are not oracular: they may help in one state while misleading the same policy in another. This makes the common privileged-teacher assumption fragile, namely that a skill-conditioned prompt can be treated as a fixed teacher for the no-skill prompt. We introduce UCOB, a framework for learning to utilize and evolve agentic skills via credit-aware on-policy bidirectional self-distillation. UCOB treats skill-conditioned and no-skill prompts as two on-policy context views of the same model, compares their return-to-go within the same task and anchor state, and uses the higher-return view as the local teacher. This local credit signal internalizes useful skill-conditioned behavior, corrects misleading skill usage, and guides task/state skill memory updates, utility-aware retrieval, and reflection self-training. Experiments on agentic tasks, including ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA, show that UCOB outperforms skill-free RL, skill-memory baselines, and self-distillation methods across model scales, with up to 23.5 and 18.0 point gains over SOTA baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop. Ablations and analyses further validate its core mechanisms, continual adaptation across environments, and modest training overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/TU2021/UCOB.

items.title: Perception-Aligned AI Outputs: End-to-End Visual Prediction for Uncertainty Communication in Clinical Decision-Making [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2205.04599v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is essential for trustworthy AI in healthcare, yet many existing methods rely on technical explanations that are difficult for clinicians and patients to interpret. We introduce Visualized Learning for Machine Learning (VL4ML), a human-centered explainability framework that communicates model predictions and uncertainty through intuitive visual representations rather than numerical or post-hoc explanations. By encoding diagnostic information in colors, patterns, and spatial structures, VL4ML enables users to interpret predictions without requiring knowledge of model internals or statistical expertise. We demonstrate the framework across multiple clinical tasks, including classification, regression, longitudinal prediction, and multimodal analysis. Its effectiveness was evaluated through a human-centered study involving 158 participants (39.2% clinical professionals) and an expert interpretability assessment. More than 79% of participants positively rated the visual explanations across evaluation dimensions, 84.0% found them more memorable than numeric outputs, and 76.9% reported faster decision-making. Over 82% successfully perceived uncertainty embedded in the visual representations without prior statistical training. No significant differences were observed between clinicians and non-clinicians or between male and female participants, indicating broad accessibility. These results suggest that VL4ML complements existing XAI and uncertainty quantification methods by providing intuitive, universally interpretable visual explanations that support transparent and trustworthy clinical decision-making.

items.title: Decoupled Alignment for Robust Plug-and-Play Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2406.01514v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a training-free safety enhancement method for aligning large language models (LLMs) without the need for supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning from human feedback. Our main idea is to provide a robust plug-and-play approach to prevent shadow alignment when models are adapted to downstream tasks. Specifically, we leverage knowledge distillation to extract alignment signals from well-aligned LLMs and inject them into shadow-aligned models via model fusion, enabling plug-and-play alignment correction. In our methodology, we employ delta debugging to identify the critical components of knowledge necessary for effective distillation. On the harmful question dataset, our method significantly enhances the average defense success rate by approximately 14.42%, reaching as high as 51.39% across 17 influenced LLMs, without compromising performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/NWULIST/DAPA.

items.title: Derivation of effective gradient flow equations and dynamical truncation of training data in Deep Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2501.07400v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We derive explicit equations governing the cumulative biases and weights in Deep Learning with ReLU activation function, based on gradient descent for the Euclidean loss in the input layer, and under the assumption that the weights are, in a precise sense, adapted to the coordinate system distinguished by the activations. We show that gradient descent corresponds to a dynamical process in the input layer, whereby clusters of data are progressively reduced in complexity ("truncated") at an exponential rate that increases with the number of data points that have already been truncated. We provide a detailed discussion of several types of solutions to the gradient flow equations. A main motivation for this work is to shed light on the interpretability question in supervised learning.

items.title: CTC: The Composite Task Challenge for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2502.00345v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The critical role of division of labor (DOL) in enhancing cooperation is well-recognized in real-world applications. Consequently, many cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods have incorporated DOL mechanisms to improve cooperation among agents. However, the lack of benchmark tasks specifically designed to evaluate and promote DOL and cooperation has limited the effective development and deployment of such mechanisms in cooperative MARL. This gap between current cooperative MARL methods and practical applications underscores the need for evaluation tasks that explicitly require DOL and cooperation. To address this gap, we propose the Composite Tasks Challenge (CTC), a suite of tasks explicitly designed to require both DOL and cooperation for successful task completion. The CTC tasks are constructed based on two core design principles: 1) DOL is a necessary condition for task success; 2) Failure in any atomic subtask results in failure of the overall task. The first principle emphasizes the necessity of DOL, while the second enforces the importance of cooperation, making both components essential for success in CTC tasks. We evaluate nine representative cooperative MARL methods on the proposed CTC tasks. Experimental results show that all methods consistently achieve zero test winning rates across all CTC tasks, highlighting the challenge of CTC tasks and the limitations of current methods. To facilitate future research, we also introduce a guiding solution that achieves non-zero test winning rates on all tasks, thereby demonstrating the solvability of the CTC tasks. However, the performance of this guiding solution remains suboptimal, further underscoring the value of CTC tasks as a challenging and meaningful testbed for advancing cooperative MARL research.

items.title: MAnchors: Memorization-Based Acceleration of Anchors via Rule Reuse and Transformation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2502.11068v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Anchors is a popular local model-agnostic explanation technique whose applicability is limited by its computational inefficiency. To address this limitation, we propose a memorization-based framework that accelerates Anchors while preserving explanation fidelity and interpretability. Our approach leverages the iterative nature of Anchors' algorithm which gradually refines an explanation until it is precise enough for a given input by storing and reusing intermediate results obtained during prior explanations. Specifically, we maintain a memory of low-precision, high-coverage rules and introduce a rule transformation framework to adapt them to new inputs: the horizontal transformation adapts a pre-trained explanation to the current input by replacing features, and the vertical transformation refines the general explanation until it is precise enough for the input. We evaluate our method across tabular, text, and image datasets, demonstrating that it significantly reduces explanation generation time while maintaining fidelity and interpretability, thereby enabling the practical adoption of Anchors in time-sensitive applications.

items.title: AuditVotes: Elevating Provable Defense for GNNs with Efficient Augmentation and Conditional Smoothing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2503.22998v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), adaptive attacks continue to challenge their robustness. Certified robustness via randomized smoothing offers provable guarantees but suffers from a severe accuracy-robustness trade-off, limiting its practical use. To bridge this gap, we introduce AuditVotes, the first framework that simultaneously achieves high clean accuracy and strong certified robustness. AuditVotes seamlessly integrates two novel components into the randomized smoothing pipeline: (1) graph rewiring augmentation, which denoises randomized graphs to recover data quality, and (2) conditional smoothing, which filters low-confidence votes to ensure prediction consistency. We establish a novel theoretical result, proving that certified robustness is preserved under arbitrary filtering functions. Designed for inductive learning, our framework generalizes to unseen nodes and applies broadly to other smoothing schemes, including de-randomized smoothing for graphs and Gaussian smoothing for images.
